title: Prohibition on sale or provision of coordinated pricing algorithms
requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to Berkeley landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for residential units in Berkeley.
quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley 
landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy 
levels that may be achieved for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.
key_value: Ban on sale/provision of coordinated pricing algorithms
coverage_conditions: Applies to algorithms using non-public Competitor Data (less than 90 days old) to recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms in coordination between a Berkeley landlord and competitors, including via third-party vendor.
exemptions: Excludes aggregated anonymous rental data reports that do not recommend prices; products used to set affordable housing rent/income limits; market research for project financing, appraisals; research, testing, or training for software development (provided competitor data is not used as an input when a recommendation is calculated).
penalty: City Attorney civil action: damages, injunctive relief, restitution, civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees and costs.
conflict_note: Ordinance was passed to print Nov. 18, 2025 (agenda dated 2025-12-02); document does not state an explicit effective date.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether algorithm uses non-public competitor data

title: SF Rent Ordinance Section 37.10C – Prohibition on algorithmic devices used to set rents or manage occupancy
requirement: Landlords and others may not sell or use algorithmic devices (software that analyzes nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rents) to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco. A tenant or the City Attorney can bring a civil action over violations.
quoted_span: The law prohibits the sale or use of such algorithmic devices and allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action if they believe an entity is in violation of the law.
key_value: Ban on sale/use of algorithmic rent-setting devices
coverage_conditions: Applies to residential units in San Francisco; 'algorithmic device' means software using algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rent for a vacant unit.
penalty: Civil action by tenant or City Attorney

title: San Diego ban on algorithmic rent-setting
requirement: Landlords may not use prohibited algorithmic pricing tools. Tenants can sue for damages, injunctive relief and penalties.
quoted_span: San Diego similarly authorizes tenant suits for damages, injunctive relief and penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, with each month and affected rental property potentially constituting a separate violation.
key_value: Up to $1,000 per violation
penalty: Up to $1,000 per violation, per month and affected property
conflict_note: Source gives effective date only as June 2025.

title: Santa Ana ban on automated rent price-fixing
requirement: Landlords may not use automated tools for anticompetitive rent price-fixing. Tenants may bring private claims.
quoted_span: Ordinance NS-3090 prohibits specified anticompetitive automated rent price-fixing; private tenant claims and up to $1,000 per violation and per month.
key_value: Up to $1,000 per violation per month
penalty: Up to $1,000 per violation and per month

title: Jersey City ban on algorithmic rent coordination services
requirement: Landlords may not use algorithmic rent coordination services. Enforcement is both public and private.
quoted_span: Prohibits a landlord’s use of algorithmic rent coordination services; includes public and private enforcement; fines up to $2,000 per day.
key_value: Fines up to $2,000 per day
penalty: Fines up to $2,000 per day
conflict_note: Source gives effective date only as June 2025.

title: Algorithmic rent fixing prohibited
requirement: Landlords may not use software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms that collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information to coordinate, recommend, or implement rents, lease terms, or occupancy levels among competing landlords. Violations can be brought in Hoboken Municipal Court by the Division of Housing or by any aggrieved private citizen.
quoted_span: Alleged violations of this chapter may be brought by the Division of Housing, or any private citizen alleging to be aggrieved, to the Hoboken Municipal Court for adjudication.
key_value: Ban on algorithmic price fixing; fine up to $2,000
penalty: Upon conviction, one or more of: penalties under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5; a fine not exceeding $2,000; community service not exceeding 90 days
exemptions: Residential dwelling unit is defined as a primary residence and excludes medical/long-term care or detention facilities.
coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords renting any residential dwelling unit in Hoboken. Nonpublic competitor information is information less than 365 days old that is not widely and readily available to the public at no cost.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Effective date not stated in text (adopted 2025-07-09).

title: Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance – ban on criminal history inquiries and adverse action
requirement: Berkeley landlords may not ask about or use criminal history in ads, applications, tenant selection, or decisions. They also may not refuse to rent, terminate a tenancy, demand a higher deposit or rent, or refuse to add a family member because of criminal history.
quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.
key_value: No criminal history inquiries or use in housing decisions
exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as primary residence; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates.
coverage_conditions: Applies to current or prospective tenants of rental housing in Berkeley, including rental assistance (e.g., Section 8) disqualification.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether an owner of record resides in a 1-3 unit property as primary residence; whether an exemption applies

penalty: Administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation, civil damages (actual damages or three times one month's rent), punitive damages, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief.
conflict_note: Page gives the City Council passage date (April 14, 2020) but no effective date.

title: No nonpayment eviction for debt below one month's Fair Market Rent
requirement: A landlord may evict for nonpayment only if the tenant owes at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent (Oakland-Fremont metro FMR) for a unit of equivalent size.
citation: Berkeley Rent Ordinance, as amended by Measure BB (Nov. 2024)
quoted_span: Eviction for nonpayment of rent is no longer permitted for rental debt of less than one month’s Fair Market Rent for a unit of equivalent size.
key_value: Rental debt must be ≥ 1 month HUD FMR
coverage_conditions: Fully or partially covered units; FMR determined for fiscal year in which rent is demanded.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Unit size and current-year FMR

title: Application screening fee cap ($30, CPI-adjusted) and actual-cost limit
requirement: A landlord can't charge more than the actual out-of-pocket cost of screening you, including the reasonable value of their time, and never more than $30 per applicant (adjusted annually for CPI since Jan. 1, 1998).
quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.
key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted annually from Jan. 1, 1998
coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords (owners of residential rental property) and their agents charging applicants, including guarantors or cosigners.
interaction: Applies notwithstanding Civ. Code § 1950.5; fee is not treated as security or an advance fee.

title: Ban on non-refundable fees to existing tenants
requirement: Owners cannot charge existing tenants a non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy, including fees for a roommate leaving or for adding or replacing a roommate in an existing household. Chapter 13.78 applies regardless of contrary lease language, and violating lease provisions are unenforceable.
quoted_span: An owner of residential rental property (or the owner’s agent) cannot charge a non-refundable fee to any existing tenant for the purpose of renewing a tenancy, in whole or in part, including any fee associated with the departure of a roommate or to request to add or replace a roommate in a pre-existing household.
coverage_conditions: Applies to all residential rental agreements (BMC 13.78.018).

title: Annual General Adjustment capped at 5%
requirement: For fully covered units, the yearly rent increase (Annual General Adjustment) set by the Rent Board can never exceed 5%, even if the CPI formula produces a higher number. Landlords with banked (unused) AGAs may still raise rent above 5% to reach the rent ceiling.
citation: Berkeley Rent Ordinance, as amended by Measure BB (Nov. 2024)
quoted_span: The maximum AGA is 5%.
key_value: AGA max 5% (CPI-based formula)
coverage_conditions: Fully covered rental units under the Berkeley Rent Ordinance.
exemptions: Cap does not prevent a landlord with banked AGAs from raising rent above 5% to reach the rent ceiling.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the unit is fully covered (vs. partially covered or exempt)

title: Return of deposit and itemized statement within 21 days
requirement: Within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates, the landlord must give the tenant an itemized statement of the basis for and amount of any deductions and return the remaining security. If repairs cannot be completed or documents are not available within 21 days, a good-faith estimate may be deducted, with final accounting within 14 days of completion.
quoted_span:
(h) (1) No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, but not earlier than the time that either the landlord or the tenant provides a notice to terminate the tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1, Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or not earlier than 60 calendar days prior to
the expiration of a fixed-term lease, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant as follows:
key_value: 21 calendar days
coverage_conditions: Residential rental security.
penalty: Landlord forfeits any claim to the security if it fails to comply in bad faith (subd. (h)(7)); statutory damages up to twice the security (subd. (m)).

title: Security deposit interest
requirement: Landlords of units fully or partially covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance must pay tenants interest on the security deposit at the end of each year, and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before year end.
citation: Berkeley Rent Ordinance (Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.76)
quoted_span: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.
key_value: Annual interest on deposit

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the unit is covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance

coverage_conditions: Units fully or partially covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance.

title: Boston Fair Chance Policy: no blanket ban on applicants with arrests or convictions
requirement: Covered affordable housing providers cannot have a blanket policy denying housing to people with arrests or convictions. They must review each applicant case by case.
citation: Boston DND Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (Feb. 2017)
quoted_span:
Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or 
land, or that have income restricted units created under the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency (BPDA) Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions.
key_value: Case-by-case review; no blanket criminal-history ban
coverage_conditions: Applies to housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or with income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; also applied to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.
exemptions: Does not apply where there is a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought, an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety, or current criminal behavior. Federal or state criminal-history requirements that conflict with the policy preempt it.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the property receives DND funding/land or has BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy income-restricted units

interaction: Federal or state law imposing a conflicting criminal history requirement preempts this policy.
conflict_note: Policy is dated February 2017; no specific effective date is stated. It is a policy/guidance document ('guidance') rather than a statute.

title: H.3744 – Home rule petition authorizing Boston rent stabilization
requirement: This bill would have let the city of Boston adopt rent stabilization. It was not enacted, so no Boston rent limits arise from it. The page does not give the text, so there are no caps or other details.
quoted_span: By Representative Montaño of Boston, a petition (accompanied by bill, House, No. 3744) of Samantha Montaño (with the approval of the mayor and city council) that the city of Boston be authorized to implement rent stabilization and tenant eviction protections.
coverage_conditions: Bill text not provided; coverage unknown.
interaction: Home rule petition: Boston needs a special law from the Legislature to act on this.
conflict_note: The page shows the bill was sent to a study order (H5035) on 9/9/2024, with no enactment. The 2023-2024 session has ended, so it is treated as failed. The page marks local approval as received. Statewide, MA G.L. c.40P bars local rent control, but that law is not in this document.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Full bill text not included in the document.

title: Boston Housing Stability Notification Act (eviction/non-renewal notice requirements)
requirement: A landlord or foreclosing owner who serves a Notice to Quit or decides not to renew a lease must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time. They must also send a copy of the Notice to Quit or non-renewal, with a Certificate of Compliance/Service, to the City's Office of Housing Stability. The ordinance is a notice and procedure rule. It does not require just cause.
citation: City of Boston Ordinances § 10-11.7 (Housing Stability Notification Act)
quoted_span:
Who has to comply with this Ordinance?
The Ordinance applies to all landlords/foreclosing owners intending to end a
tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in the City of Boston.
key_value: Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources delivered with Notice to Quit; copy to Office of Housing Stability
coverage_conditions: Applies to all landlords/foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy in Boston.
exemptions: Residences in a hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility; and in a non-profit facility whose primary purpose is short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug, or other substance abuse.
penalty: Enforced by Inspectional Services Department: 1st offense warning; 2nd and subsequent offenses $300 per day. A violation does not halt the eviction process.
interaction: Requirements cannot be waived; lease terms purporting to waive them are void and unenforceable.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Property must not be an exempt facility (hospital, nursing/health facility, non-profit substance abuse treatment facility).

title: Source-of-income discrimination prohibited in housing
requirement: A landlord can't discriminate against or harass an applicant or tenant because of their source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, HUD-VASH vouchers, and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Landlords also can't advertise a preference or limitation based on source of income.
quoted_span: (a) For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.
key_value: Source of income is a protected class
exemptions: Asking about the level or source of income is not discrimination (§ 12955(p)(2)).
coverage_conditions: Applies to owners of housing accommodations; 'source of income' means lawful, verifiable income paid to a tenant, their representative, or to the landlord on the tenant's behalf, including federal, state or local assistance and housing subsidies.

title: California Tenant Protection Act – Just Cause Required to Terminate Tenancy
requirement: After a tenant has lived in a unit continuously and lawfully for 12 months, the landlord can end the tenancy only for a legally listed at-fault or no-fault reason, and that reason must be stated in the written termination notice. If additional adult tenants were added before an existing tenant reached 24 months, protection applies once all tenants have 12+ months or any tenant has 24+ months.
quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
key_value: Just cause after 12 months of occupancy

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether a local just-cause ordinance applies; tenancy length; whether unit is alienable separate from other units (single-family/condo) and owner type; owner-occupancy/shared-facilities status; affordable-housing restrictions

coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property after 12 months of continuous lawful occupancy (24 months if adult tenants were added). At-fault just causes include nonpayment, material lease breach, nuisance, waste, refusal to renew, criminal activity, unlawful sublet, refusal of entry, unlawful use, failure to vacate after employment ends or after tenant's own notice. No-fault just causes: owner/family move-in, withdrawal from rental market, government/court vacate or habitability order, demolition or substantial remodel.
exemptions: Transient/tourist hotels; nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care, RCFE or adult residential facility housing; school dormitories; tenant shares bathroom/kitchen with owner-occupant; single-family owner-occupied residences renting no more than two units/bedrooms, and mobilehomes in that category; owner-occupied duplex; housing with certificate of occupancy within previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable property (e.g., condo/single-family) whose owner is not a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member and where written exemption notice was given; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; homeowners of a mobilehome.
penalty: Notice is void; owner who recovers possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, attorney's fees and costs at court's discretion, and up to three times actual damages (plus punitive damages) if willful or with oppression, fraud, or malice. AG, city attorney or county counsel may seek injunctive relief.
interaction: Yields to qualifying local just-cause ordinances (adopted on or before Sept 1, 2019, or more protective ones adopted/amended later); a property is not subject to both.
conflict_note: Section became operative April 1, 2024 (original AB 1482 protections began Jan 1, 2020); most recently amended by AB 1529 effective Jan 1, 2026. Section is repealed as of Jan 1, 2030 by its own terms.

title: California statewide rent cap (SB 567 version of Tenant Protection Act)
requirement: Landlords cannot raise rent over any 12-month period by more than 5% plus the local percentage change in cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower. The cap is measured from the lowest gross rent charged in the prior 12 months, excluding accepted discounts or concessions. Rent increase notices must follow Civ. Code § 827.
quoted_span: Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.
key_value: 5% + CPI change, max 10%

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether housing is deed-restricted affordable, a dormitory, or subject to a stricter local rent control; whether the required exemption notice was given; whether a mobilehome homeowner.

coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property (including mobilehome park units) not exempt under subdivision (d). Applies to mobilehome tenancies only for increases on or after Feb 18, 2021; otherwise to increases on or after March 15, 2019.
exemptions: Deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; dormitories; housing under stricter local rent control; housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable property (e.g., single-family homes, condos) if owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management and written exemption notice is given; duplex where owner occupies one unit as principal residence (neither unit an ADU/JADU); mobilehome homeowners.
interaction: Does not preempt or expand local rent control consistent with Civ. Code ch. 2.7 (§ 1954.50 et seq.); stricter local rent control controls. Repealed as of January 1, 2030 by its own terms.
penalty: Civil action by tenant for injunctive relief, damages equal to the overcharge, discretionary attorney's fees and costs, and up to treble damages for willful, oppressive, fraudulent or malicious conduct; Attorney General, city attorney or county counsel may enforce; 3-year limitations period; waivers void.

title: Common pricing algorithm prohibited as part of a conspiracy or combination to restrain trade (AB 325)
requirement: It is illegal to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm (software or other method used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend or influence prices) as part of a contract, trust-like combination, or conspiracy to restrain trade. Landlords and rent-pricing software vendors can be liable under the Cartwright Act.
quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
key_value: Ban on common pricing algorithms used in anticompetitive combinations
interaction: Does not impair or limit the applicability of other antitrust laws (§ 16729(c)).
penalty: Violations of the Cartwright Act; the bill digest notes violation is punishable as a crime.
coverage_conditions: Applies to any 'person' (as defined in Section 16702, excluding end consumers) using or distributing a methodology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or influence a price or commercial term. Not limited to housing on its face. The chaptered text does not state an effective date; 2026-01-01 reflects the general effective date for non-urgency statutes chaptered in 2025.

title: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance: uniform, reasonable tenant selection standards
requirement: Landlords, sellers and rental agents may screen applicants using any reasonable standard, but they must apply it equally and uniformly to all applicants. Tenant selection may be based on ability to pay the rent and ability to take care of the apartment and respect the rights of others.
citation: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance, Cambridge Municipal Code ch. 14.04
quoted_span: Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.
key_value: Reasonable standard applied uniformly to all applicants
coverage_conditions: Applies to renting and viewing apartments and related housing transactions in Cambridge.
exemptions: Exemption for 2-family dwellings when the owner lives there.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the owner lives in the 2-family dwelling

penalty: Commission may levy civil fines of up to $300 per violation, file criminal or civil complaints, and seek injunctive relief, damages and expenses.

title: Cambridge policy order to ban use of algorithmic rent-pricing software by property managers
requirement: The City Council has started the process of banning residential property management companies from using third-party algorithmic or AI-driven pricing tools to set rents. It is not yet law. The city manager must present draft policy options or ordinance language to the council later this term.
citation: Cambridge City Council Policy Order (adopted June 2026; no ordinance number assigned)
quoted_span: City council also unanimously passed a policy order initiating steps to ban residential property management companies from contracting companies that use algorithmic and AI-driven models to recommend what they should charge for rent.
key_value: Proposed ban on algorithmic rent-recommendation software
coverage_conditions: Applies to residential property management companies that contract with algorithmic or AI pricing providers. The article describes targets as large or corporate owners and managers.
interaction: Complements pending Massachusetts state bills on the same practice. The article does not describe any preemption.
conflict_note: The article is dated June 25, 2026 but the document header says October 3, 2026. As of 2026-10-01 only a policy order directing staff to draft options exists. No ordinance has been enacted.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Ordinance language not yet drafted, so unit-count thresholds and definitions are unknown.

title: Annual rent increase cap: lesser of 5% or CPI
requirement: At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not raise rent by more than 5% or the CPI percentage change, whichever is less. Only one cost-of-living increase is allowed in any 12-month period regardless of the number of tenants.
quoted_span: At the expiration of a lease or at the termination of a lease of a periodic tenant, no landlord may request or receive a percentage increase in rent which is greater than 5% or the percentage difference between the consumer price index three months prior to the expiration or termination of the lease and three months prior to the commencement of the lease term, whichever is less.
key_value: Lesser of 5% or CPI
coverage_conditions: Dwellings covered by Chapter 155; for periodic tenants or leases under one year, no more than one increase exceeding the cap in any 12-month period.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Exemptions not in excerpt.

title: Jersey City Rent Control Ordinance (Chapter 260) – 1-4 unit exemption
requirement: Rent for covered Jersey City apartments is regulated under the city's Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260, administered by the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations. Properties with 1-4 units are exempt; tenants can ask about a property's rent control status, and can file an Illegal Rent Petition if they believe their rent is illegal.
quoted_span: (Please Note: All 1-4 Unit Properties are exempt from rent control)

coverage.other_missing_fact: Other exemptions exist under the ordinance (via Rent Control Exemption Request) but are not detailed on this page; the allowable increase percentage/CPI cap is not stated.

coverage_conditions: Applies to rental properties with 5 or more units, subject to other exemptions in the ordinance.
exemptions: All 1-4 unit properties are exempt; owners may submit a Rent Control Exemption Request for other permitted exemptions.

title: LA source-of-income discrimination ban: refusal to rent, renew, or terminate tenancy
requirement: Landlords cannot refuse to rent, renew, or continue a tenancy, refuse to sign Section 8 or other assistance paperwork, or serve a termination notice because of a tenant's or applicant's source of income, including vouchers and other rental assistance.
quoted_span: Based upon a person’s source of income, refuse to rent or lease, or to continue to rent or lease, a housing accommodation; refuse to enter into or renew a rental agreement, lease or housing assistance payment contract; refuse to execute any documents required to enter into or renew a rental agreement, lease or housing assistance payment contract; serve a notice of termination of tenancy; seek to terminate or terminate a tenancy; or otherwise deny or withhold, a housing accommodation or housing services or amenities.
key_value: No discrimination based on source of income (incl. Section 8 vouchers)
coverage_conditions: Applies to any person offering for rent, renting, or listing a housing accommodation in the City of Los Angeles; includes dwelling units, guest rooms, duplexes, condos, single-family homes, and mobile homes. Source of income includes any lawful income, rental assistance, subsidy or financial aid.
penalty: Civil action for injunctive relief and damages; punitive damages of no less than three times actual damages or three times one month's rent, whichever is higher; attorney fees and costs; violation is an affirmative defense to unlawful detainer.

title: Motion directing report on feasibility of banning algorithm-based rent-setting software
requirement: A City Council motion asks the Los Angeles Housing Department to report on how many owners and managers use algorithm-based software to set rents and whether the City could ban it. No ban is in effect. Landlords are not yet restricted by this motion.
citation: L.A. City Council File No. 24-1031 (Motion of Councilmember Hutt, Sept. 3, 2024)
quoted_span:
MOTION
SEP 0 3 2024
I THEREFORE MOVE that the City Council instruct the Los Angeles Housing Department to 
report on the number of ownership and management entities that are using algorithm-based 
software to establish rents and the feasibility of instituting a ban on the use of this software to set 
rents in the City.
key_value: Report-back on feasibility of a ban (no ban enacted)
coverage_conditions: Applies to ownership and management entities using algorithm-based software to establish rents in the City of Los Angeles, if a ban is later adopted.
conflict_note: The motion only requests a report and feasibility study. It is not an enacted ordinance. It also references San Francisco's July 2024 legislation banning such tools, but gives no citation for it.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Text of any eventual ordinance, including scope and exemptions, is not available.

title: No-fault evictions: LAHD declaration and notice filing under RSO/JCO
requirement: Before a no-fault eviction in an RSO or JCO unit, the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD and pay relocation assistance. The termination notice can only be served after the declaration is filed, and a copy must be filed with LAHD within 3 days of service.
quoted_span:
Failure to file the Landlord Declaration with the LAHD makes the eviction a 
violation of the RSO or JCO.
coverage_conditions: Units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or Just Cause Ordinance (JCO).
key_value: File declaration before notice; copy of notice to LAHD within 3 days (3 business days for demolition-for-new-construction)
penalty: Eviction without filing is a violation of the RSO or JCO.
conflict_note: Bulletin A says a copy of the notice must be filed within 3 days; Bulletin B (demolition for new construction) says within 3 business days.

title: RSO utility pass-through increase eliminated
requirement: Effective February 2, 2026, landlords of RSO units can no longer add an extra percentage to the rent increase for utilities.
quoted_span: Effective February 2, 2026, the landlord can no longer include an additional percentage increase for utilities.
key_value: No additional utility percentage

title: LARSO security deposit interest must be paid monthly or yearly
requirement: Landlords of rent-stabilized (LARSO) units in the City of Los Angeles must pay tenants interest on security deposits, either monthly or yearly, as a direct payment or a rent credit. The landlord must tell the tenant in writing which method it chose; waiting until the end of the tenancy does not comply.
quoted_span: The landlord may elect to pay the accrued interest on a monthly or yearly basis.
key_value: Annual City-set interest rate (4.320% for calendar year 2025); paid monthly or yearly
coverage_conditions: Properties in the City of Los Angeles subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (LARSO).
penalty: Non-compliance can be used as a defense in eviction proceedings, risking loss of eviction cases.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the unit is subject to LARSO

title: H.5222 - An Act relative to preventing algorithmic rent fixing in the rental housing market
requirement: Massachusetts bill H.5222 would address algorithmic rent fixing in the rental housing market. It is not law. It was reported favorably by the Housing Committee on 3/12/2026 and sent to House Ways and Means. The captured page does not include the bill text, so its specific requirements are unknown.
quoted_span: An Act relative to preventing algorithmic rent fixing in the rental housing market
conflict_note: Bill page shows H.5222 as a new draft of H1564. Only the title and history were captured, not the operative text.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Bill text not captured; scope, definitions, and exemptions unknown.

title: An Act prohibiting algorithmic rent setting (S.2983, 194th General Court)
requirement: Bill S.2983 would prohibit algorithmic rent setting in Massachusetts. It is only a proposal: the Housing Committee reported it favorably on 3/12/2026 and sent it to Senate Ways and Means. It is not law, and the page does not give the bill's operative text.
citation: Mass. Bill S.2983, 194th Gen. Court (2025-2026 Session)
quoted_span: An Act prohibiting algorithmic rent setting
conflict_note: S.2983 is a new draft of S.994 and S.1016 (the Preventing Algorithmic Rent Fixing in the Rental Housing Market Act). The captured page shows only the bill history, not the bill text, so scope, definitions, exemptions and penalties cannot be confirmed.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Operative text of the bill is not included in the captured document.

title: MA G.L. c. 40P § 4 – General prohibition on local rent control
requirement: Cities and towns in Massachusetts may not enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. A narrow exception lets a municipality that accepts chapter 40P adopt only voluntary, compensated rent control for owners of ten or more units with fair market rent of $400 or less.
quoted_span: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:
key_value: Local rent control prohibited (narrow voluntary, compensated exception)
coverage_conditions: Applies to all cities and towns in MA. The exception applies only to municipalities that accept chapter 40P. Regulation may apply only to units owned by a person or entity owning ten or more rental units, and with fair market rent not exceeding $400. Compliance by owners is voluntary after six months from initial adoption. The municipality must compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and the controlled rent.
exemptions: Exception for municipalities accepting ch. 40P; regulation may not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal of properties from regulation; may not apply to units owned by a person or entity owning fewer than ten rental units or having fair market rent exceeding $400.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the municipality has accepted ch. 40P; unit fair market rent (must not exceed $400)

title: Source-of-income and housing subsidy discrimination barred
requirement: Landlords and others offering rental accommodations may not refuse or discriminate against someone because they receive public assistance or a housing subsidy (such as a voucher or rental assistance), or because of the requirements of those programs.
quoted_span: For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, because the individual is such a recipient, or because of any requirement of such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program.
key_value: No discrimination based on public assistance or housing subsidy
coverage_conditions: Applies to any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations.

title: Notice to quit for nonpayment of rent under a written lease; right to cure
requirement: If rent due under a written lease isn't paid, the landlord may end the lease with 14 days' written notice to quit. The tenant can stop the termination by paying all rent due, with interest and costs, on or before the answer day in the landlord's possession action.
quoted_span: Upon the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due under a written lease, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the lease, unless the tenant, on or before the day the answer is due, in an action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises, pays or tenders to the landlord or to his attorney all rent then due, with interest and costs of suit.
key_value: 14 days' written notice to quit for nonpayment
coverage_conditions: Applies to tenancies under a written lease where rent due is unpaid.
conflict_note: This is a nonpayment termination procedure, not a general statewide just-cause eviction requirement; Massachusetts has no comprehensive just-cause statute in this text. If nonpayment was caused by a delay by a government agency in mailing or delivering a subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days and treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent, interest and costs are tendered in that time.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the tenancy is under a written lease

title: Cap on upfront payments and security deposit (first month's rent)
requirement: At or before the start of a tenancy, a landlord or agent may only collect first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit no more than one month's rent, and the cost of a key and lock. After the tenancy begins, the landlord cannot demand rent in advance beyond the current month or a deposit above the legal limit.
quoted_span: At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, no lessor or agent of the lessor may require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay, to the lessor or to an agent of the lessor, any amount in excess of the following:
key_value: Security deposit max 1 month's rent (plus first month, last month, key/lock cost)
exemptions: Does not apply to leases or rentals of 100 days or less for vacation or recreational purposes (§ 15B(9)).
coverage_conditions: Residential real property leases and tenancies; deposit must be held per subsection (3) and a statement of condition given per subsection (2).
conflict_note: Two versions of clause (1)(b) are published: text effective until Aug 1, 2025 (applies to 'lessor' only) and text effective Aug 1, 2025 (adds 'agent of the lessor' per 2025, c. 9). As of 2026-10-01 the amended text governs; the substantive 1-month cap is unchanged.
penalty: Treble damages for violations of certain subsection 6 clauses; forfeiture of right to retain deposit (see §15B(6)-(7)).

coverage.other_missing_fact: Lease length (exempt if 100 days or less for vacation/recreation)

title: Landlords limited to first, last, security deposit and lock fee; application fees barred
requirement: Before a tenancy begins, a Massachusetts landlord (lessor) may only require first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit, and a lock-change fee. Application, screening, pet, cleaning, amenity and other fees are not allowed to be charged by landlords.
key_value: No application fee (only first, last, security, lock)
coverage_conditions: Applies to lessors/landlords; the article advises that landlors who are also brokers, or who require applicants to pay a third-party screening service, risk liability.
exemptions: Licensed brokers may charge fees under broker regulations (254 CMR 7).
penalty: In Perry v. Equity Residential Management (federal district court, 2014), tenants were awarded treble damages and attorney's fees.
conflict_note: Source is a secondary trade-association article; the Samia v. McElaney (1983) Housing Court decision and the absence of appellate authority leave uncertain whether landlords who are also licensed brokers may charge fees.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the person charging is a landlord or a separately operating licensed broker

title: Initiative Petition 25-21 statewide rent increase cap (blocked from ballot)
requirement: The proposed initiative would have capped annual rent increases statewide at the lesser of CPI or 5%. The SJC ruled in Cella v. Attorney General that it cannot appear on the November 2026 ballot, so it is not law.
citation: Initiative Petition 25-21; Cella v. Attorney General, SJC-13893
quoted_span: Under the proposed law, annual rent increases would have been limited to the lesser of the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index or 5%.
key_value: Lesser of CPI increase or 5%
exemptions: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units, newly constructed units less than 10 years old, certain publicly regulated units, short-term rentals, and dwelling units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or nonprofit purposes.
coverage_conditions: Would have applied to most residential rental units statewide.
conflict_note: The blog post is dated June 23, 2026, but a related recent-post blurb refers to the SJC ruling as 'June 24, 2026'. The ruling date is inconsistently reported. Proponents say the defect is fixable and may re-file.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether unit is publicly regulated, a short-term rental, or in an educational/religious/nonprofit facility

title: FAIR Act: Landlords barred from using rent-pricing coordinators
requirement: A landlord (or its agent or subcontractor) may not pay for or otherwise use the services of a coordinator, meaning algorithmic rent-setting software or devices that pool competitors' nonpublic data to set or recommend rents, lease terms or occupancy levels.
key_value: Unlawful to use a coordinator's services
penalty: Violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act; enforcement provisions of N.J.S.A. 56:9-6 through 9-17 remain applicable (§5).
exemptions: Coordinating function excludes research/statistical/testing use not used to set terms, free public rent estimates, equal-terms real estate brokerage databases that do not set or recommend terms, and government affordability controls.
coverage_conditions: Applies to residential dwelling units (houses, apartments, accessory units used as a primary residence in NJ); excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, detention/correctional facilities.
interaction: In addition to the NJ Antitrust Act; municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.
conflict_note: Effective date computed from §9 (first day of the twelfth month after July 20, 2026 enactment) as 2027-07-01; the text does not state a calendar date.

title: Fair Chance in Housing Act: no criminal record inquiries before conditional offer
requirement: A landlord cannot ask about your criminal record, on an application or orally or in writing, until after making you a conditional offer. Narrow exceptions apply for methamphetamine manufacture convictions in federally assisted housing and lifetime sex offender registration.
quoted_span:
(2)
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.
key_value: No criminal record inquiry before conditional offer
exemptions: Dwelling units in owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.
coverage_conditions: Applies to housing providers offering rental dwelling units.
penalty: Civil penalty up to $1,000 (first violation), $5,000 (second within 5 years), $10,000 (two or more within 7 years); enforced by Division on Civil Rights, no court action by individuals.
conflict_note: Effective date computed from 'first day of the seventh month next following' enactment on June 18, 2021; the text does not state a calendar date.

title: Anti-Eviction Act: good cause required to evict or not renew
requirement: A landlord can evict a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a good cause listed in the Anti-Eviction Act. The landlord must prove the grounds in court, and the tenant does not have to move until the court enters a judgment for possession.
quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
key_value: Good cause required
coverage_conditions: Most residential rentals, including single-family homes, mobile homes, apartments and rooming/boarding houses.
exemptions: May not apply to owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; hotel/motel guests and transient or seasonal tenants (unless the hotel is their only residence); units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member who permanently occupies them.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the owner lives in the building; whether the tenancy is seasonal or transient

title: Return of deposit within 30 days
requirement: The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Deductions can cover damage beyond normal wear and tear and money due under the lease, and must be itemized by registered or certified mail.
quoted_span:
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant ( N.J.S.A.
key_value: 30 days
penalty: Double the wrongfully withheld amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Residential rental application fee capped at $50
requirement: A landlord or agent cannot charge more than $50 for an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental. If you were overcharged, the wrongfully charged amount is to be taken from the penalty and returned to you.
quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
penalty: Up to $500 first offense, up to $750 second offense, up to $1,000 each subsequent offense; enforced through summary proceedings in Special Civil Part on complaint of the Director of Consumer Affairs or Attorney General; wrongfully charged amount remitted to the applicant from the penalty.
exemptions: Dwelling units in a one-family or two-family dwelling offered for rent; NJ Real Estate Commission licensees, unless the licensee is the landlord of the property.
coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property applications for dwelling purposes.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the unit is in a one-family or two-family dwelling (exempt) and whether the person charging is a NJ Real Estate Commission licensee who is not the landlord (exempt).

conflict_note: Act takes effect on the first day of the fourth month after enactment (approved January 20, 2026), computed as May 1, 2026; the text does not state a calendar date.

title: No statewide rent control; municipalities may enact rent control
requirement: New Jersey has no statewide cap on rent. Only towns that have passed a rent control or rent leveling ordinance limit increases, so check with your local rent control board or municipal clerk.
citation: Truth in Renting guide (NJ DCA); Iganamort v. Borough of Fort Lee, 120 N.J. Super. 286 (1973)
quoted_span: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents.
key_value: No state cap; local ordinances only
coverage_conditions: Applies where no municipal rent control ordinance covers the unit.
exemptions: Units covered by a local ordinance follow the ordinance.
interaction: Municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances; locally created boards enforce them.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the municipality has a rent control ordinance covering the unit

title: Newark rent control: annual increase capped at CPI change, max 4%
requirement: At lease expiration or the end of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not raise rent by more than the CPI-U (NY-Northern NJ-Long Island) percentage change measured from 15 months before to 3 months before the month of the increase. The increase can never exceed 4%.
quoted_span: In no case shall the allowable rent increase exceed 4%.
key_value: CPI change, max 4%
coverage_conditions: Applies to all multiple dwellings and housing spaces covered by Chapter 19:2.
exemptions: Public housing; hotel/motel transient space; commercial space; newly constructed multiple dwellings and vacant dwellings per §§ 19:2-18.1 and 19:2-18.2; certain federally/state rehabilitated Section 8 units; units under governmental agency rent-regulation contracts.
penalty: Fine of $100 to $2,000 and/or up to 90 days imprisonment per violation; each housing space is a separate violation (§ 19:2-19).

title: Newark Ban the Box: Criminal history inquiry only after formal application
requirement: A landlord or broker cannot ask about or consider your criminal history until you have submitted a formal application. If you volunteer information about your record on your own, they may discuss it.
quoted_span: Inquiry into and consideration of any applicant's criminal history shall take place only after the applicant has submitted a formal application.
key_value: No criminal history inquiry before formal application
coverage_conditions: Applies to any rental, lease, or sublease of real property in Newark by a landlord or real estate broker.
exemptions: Rental of a single apartment in a two-family dwelling where the owner lives in the other unit; rental of rooms in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling; where federal or state law requires or permits consideration of criminal history; property in government programs encouraging housing for people with criminal histories (§§ 2:31-1, 2:31-8).
penalty: Fine up to $500 for a first violation and up to $1,000 for each subsequent violation (§ 2:31-9).

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the unit is in an owner-occupied one- or two-family dwelling; whether federal/state law requires criminal history consideration

title: Just cause required to terminate a tenancy
requirement: A landlord covered by the ordinance cannot end a tenancy unless there is an at-fault or no-fault just cause. The ordinance is intended to be consistent with Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2.
quoted_span: A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause.
key_value: Just cause required (at-fault or no-fault)
coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property with a tenancy (more than 30 days), unless exempt under § 98.0703.
exemptions: See § 98.0703 exemptions.
interaction: Consistent with and in addition to state law (Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2); rights are in addition to any existing state or federal rights.
penalty: Wrongful eviction damages of at least three times actual economic damages; notice void for noncompliance (§ 98.0709, § 98.0710).
conflict_note: Amended effective 2024-03-28 (O-21769); original effective 2023-06-24 (O-21647).

title: San Francisco Fair Chance Ordinance (affordable housing)
requirement: San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance protects residents with an arrest or conviction history in affordable housing decisions. The page gives no further detail on what housing providers may or may not consider.
citation: Not stated in source document (referred to only as San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance)
quoted_span: San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance protects residents with arrest or conviction history in affordable housing decisions.
coverage_conditions: Page describes it as applying to affordable housing decisions; no further coverage details given.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Page is a landing page with only a one-line description; the ordinance text, citation, effective date and specific requirements are not provided.

title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause eviction requirement (Section 37.9(a))
requirement: A landlord of a unit covered by the SF Rent Ordinance can evict only for one of 17 listed just causes, and that reason must be the dominant motive for the eviction. Expiration of a lease or a change in ownership is not just cause.
quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.
key_value: 17 just cause reasons
coverage_conditions: Units covered by the SF Rent Ordinance, including some tenancies exempt from rent increase limits (units first receiving a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies, and some tenancies regulated by another government agency).
exemptions: Not stated on this page beyond the coverage description; some tenancies exempt from rent increase limits remain subject to the eviction provisions.
penalty: Landlord who evicts or tries to evict unlawfully may face substantial civil and/or criminal liability.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Whether the tenancy is covered by the Rent Ordinance or an exempt category

title: SF Rent Board allowable annual rent increase (Mar 2026–Feb 2027)
requirement: For rent-controlled units, a landlord may raise rent by no more than 1.6% for the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. The prior periods were 1.4% (2025–26) and 1.7% (2024–25).
quoted_span: 1.6% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027
coverage_conditions: Units covered by the SF Rent Ordinance; the page does not state coverage criteria.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Coverage criteria (e.g., construction date, unit type) not stated in this document

title: SF security deposit interest rate (Mar 2026–Feb 2027)
requirement: Landlords must pay tenants interest on security deposits at 4.2% for the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. Prior rates were 5.0% (2025–26) and 5.2% (2024–25).
quoted_span: 4.2% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027
key_value: 4.2% annual interest

coverage.other_missing_fact: Coverage criteria not stated in this document

title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization Ordinance – annual rent cap
requirement: Annual rent increases cannot exceed the lower of 3% or 80% of the 12-month change in CPI. If CPI is negative, no increase is allowed. The City publishes the allowable increase by June 30 each year, effective September 1. Owners must give written notice of the ordinance and tenant rights at lease start or with any rent-increase notice.
citation: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization Ordinance (adopted 2021; no codified section cited in source)
quoted_span: Increase in residential rents are limited to the lower of 3% per year, or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period.
key_value: Lower of 3% or 80% of CPI change; no increase if CPI negative
exemptions: Residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995, and mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990.

coverage.other_missing_fact: Mobile home spaces: offered for rent date (before/after 1990-01-01)

coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property and mobile home park spaces in Santa Ana not otherwise exempt.
conflict_note: Source page says the Nov. 19 effective date is 2021; page retrieved in 2026 so the ordinance is treated as in force.

title: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
requirement: After a tenant has occupied for 30 days, an owner may end a tenancy only for a just cause stated in a written notice. For at-fault causes, the owner must first give notice of the violation and time to fix it. Owners must notify tenants of the protections.
citation: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance (adopted 2021; no codified section cited in source)
quoted_span: After 30 days, an owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in a written notice.
key_value: Just cause required after 30 days
exemptions: Housing produced in the last 15 years; deed-restricted affordable housing; hotel and transient occupancy; hospital and care facilities; dormitories; and other shared living quarters.
coverage_conditions: At-fault causes include nonpayment, material lease breach, nuisance, criminal activity; no-fault causes include owner move-in, withdrawal from market, demolition or substantial remodel.
